skill.name: agentic-structure
skill.description: Collaborative programming framework for production-ready development. Use it to guide feature planning, code quality, security decisions, error handling, comments, discussions, and knowledge gaps.
skill.summary: Guides AI-assisted development with structured workflow, coding, security, error handling, and collaboration rules.
skill.author: BackGwa

- **Avoid over-fragmentation** - Don't split related code just for the sake of small files
### Avoid Over-Fragmentation
- Avoid scattering related code by type only (all models in one folder, all controllers in another)
- Avoid copy-paste duplication when the logic is meaningfully the same.
- Avoid swallowing errors; when you catch, either:
- Validate inputs early to prevent invalid states from propagating.
- Be mindful of resource safety (memory, file handles, network connections) and avoid leaks.

content.value_statement: AI coding agents need clear rules for safe, maintainable implementation. This skill provides structured guidelines for planning, coding, security, errors, comments, and knowledge gaps.
actual_capabilities: Guides feature work through core logic, integration, and interface priorities.
Defines when to ask clarifying questions or present implementation options.
Provides coding standards for naming, file organization, refactoring, and abstraction decisions.
Gives secure coding guidance for secrets, hashing, authentication, rate limits, uploads, and dependencies.
Defines error handling practices for validation, retries, fail-fast behavior, and safe user messages.
Provides a knowledge gap protocol for references, search documentation, and user-provided information.
limitations: It provides process guidance and does not execute code or run tests by itself.
The agent must read the relevant guideline files for each task.
Some recommendations need adaptation to the project framework and team conventions.
It does not replace manual security review for production systems.

use_cases.title: Plan a New Feature
use_cases.description: Use the development process rules to split work into core logic, integration, and interface steps.

use_cases.title: Guide an AI Coding Session
use_cases.description: Use the selection matrix to choose the right guidance before writing code or asking questions.

use_cases.title: Standardize Team Expectations
use_cases.description: Use the coding, security, comment, and error handling rules as a shared development baseline.

prompt_templates.title: Start a Simple Change
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner request for a clear implementation path.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use agentic-structure to plan this small feature. Identify the core logic first, then the validation step, then the interface work.

prompt_templates.title: Resolve Ambiguous Requirements
prompt_templates.scenario: A request includes unclear success criteria.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the discussion guidelines to find ambiguities in this request. Ask only the clarification questions needed before implementation.

prompt_templates.title: Review Security-Sensitive Work
prompt_templates.scenario: A change handles user input, secrets, authentication, or uploads.
prompt_templates.prompt: Apply the security and error handling guidelines to this implementation. Identify risks, required safeguards, and validation checks.

prompt_templates.title: Run a Full Agentic Workflow
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced task that spans design, implementation, validation, and documentation.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use agentic-structure across this task. Select relevant guidelines, present trade-offs, implement in small validated steps, and summarize decisions.

output_examples.input: Add a user profile import feature with unclear file format support.
output: Clarification needed: supported file types, maximum file size, and failure behavior.
Implementation order: parser rules, validation, storage integration, then interface feedback.
Security checks: type allowlist, size limits, safe filenames, and isolated storage.

output_examples.input: Refactor a large service file that mixes validation, database writes, and notifications.
output: Split by cohesive responsibility only where it improves navigation and testability.
Keep existing public behavior stable while extracting focused units.
Validate with existing tests and one manual path that exercises the refactored flow.

output_examples.input: Handle errors from a payment provider integration.
output: Classify transient, validation, authorization, and provider failures separately.
Retry only recoverable failures with limits and backoff.
Return user-safe messages while preserving operator context in logs.

best_practices: Read only the guideline files relevant to the current task.
Validate after each implementation step before expanding scope.
Treat security guidance as highest priority when guidelines conflict.
anti_patterns: Applying every guideline mechanically without considering project context.
Skipping clarification when requirements have multiple valid interpretations.
Treating the skill as a replacement for tests, code review, or security review.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It helps AI coding agents plan, implement, validate, and discuss software changes using structured engineering guidelines.

faq.question: Does it write code automatically?
faq.answer: No. It guides how an agent should approach coding tasks, but the agent still performs the actual implementation.

faq.question: When should I use the security guidelines?
faq.answer: Use them when work touches secrets, user input, authentication, authorization, uploads, dependencies, or production exposure.

faq.question: Can it help with unclear requirements?
faq.answer: Yes. It provides triggers and question patterns for resolving ambiguity before implementation starts.

faq.question: Does it require external tools?
faq.answer: No. The skill is documentation-based and uses repository reading tools to load the relevant guideline files.

faq.question: Is it suitable for team standards?
faq.answer: Yes. Teams can use it as a baseline for coding style, collaboration, security expectations, and error handling practices.
